newsitem.title: SPAIN: OPINION - PUMPING UP EUROPE FOR EMU, BY HENRIK LUMHOLDT.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - PUMPING UP EUROPE FOR EMU, BY HENRIK LUMHOLDT.

text.p: Chief Economist, Bank of America, Madrid

MADRID, Aug 11 - It must have been a frustrating experience for European leaders back in early 1992 to see that the EMU project they had just agreed on in late 1991 was already being jeopardised by a general slowdown in the European economy a few months later.

And, as if the concomitant gloom this caused among European voters was not enough, the situation triggered a general currency crisis of hitherto unknown dimensions. Long gone was the talk of a future EMU.

Now attention was on saving that much lesser institution which was the ERM, a goal which could only be achieved by redefining its scope. It is understandable therefore that leaders are bent on not repeating that mistake this time around, close to the final stages in the political process towards EMU.

The fact that the Maastricht criteria are formally attached to 1997 is of course a consideration. Fiscal policies must necessarily be rather tight across the board this year to help bring public sector deficits to the required three percent of GDP.

But given the fairly benign inflation situation in most countries this effort can at least be countered by relatively cheap money. Lax monetary policies are fairly easy to justify in the core of Europe and they help significantly in bringing about that boost in economic growth which will ensure compliance with the public deficit criterion via tax revenues.
In this context, understand cheap money in the widest possible sense: both the level of interest rates and the external value of the soon-to-exist euro is in question.
Had this whole process been an exercise in one-period economics most concerns would probably be misplaced. But looking into 1998 a picture shapes which may be less reassuring.

Europe has signed a Stability Pact designed to ensure that public sector deficits do not exceed the three percent of GDP target in years to come, and it would therefore be ideal if growth in 1998 were sufficiently high to keep deficit levels on target, while allowing for some relaxation of fiscal policies. Indeed starting off EMU on a strong note might do away with some of that gloom affecting parts of the European voters. But there is no Stability Pact on inflation.

Enter the Bundesbank and the future European Central Bank. Hopefully, EMU will not start off as a clash between the desire for economic growth to reduce unemployment and the likely monetary orthodoxy which will be embedded in the structure of the ECB. But what is the outlook until it takes charge?

It is widely believed that the Bundesbank has only relatively limited scope for action this year with unemployment at record highs, inflation still at low (if slightly increasing) levels and with a somewhat unresolved political scenario in the background. But if the US dollar continues its uptrend the risk that import price pressures take root in domestic prices towards the end of the year objectively exists.

The dominant interpretation of the strength of the dollar is that the future euro will be a weak currency due to the participation in EMU of countries like Italy and Spain. This would imply that participation by these countries will mean less rigour in future monetary policy.

It is possible to present the rather different interpretation of the strength of the dollar that it is a reflection of a desire (perceived by the markets) to drive economic growth in Europe to maximum levels for the reasons discussed earlier, riding roughshod over Europe's famous structural rigidities.

A less friendly interpretation is that there is, implicit in the currency market's response, a sign of less confidence in the longer term viability of this strategy. Looked at from this perspective currency markets have been ahead, and bond markets are beginning to face up to a new and less friendly scene.

Guessing what course of action the Bundesbank will take now is getting harder reflecting, perhaps, the unenviable position of this well-managed institution in the run-up to EMU. The uncomfortable outlook is that neither no response, nor a symbolic response, nor a strong response from the Buba looks likely to entirely remove the fears haunting bonds.

The (more likely) first two risk signalling too clear a go-ahead for dollar bulls, leaving the underlying problem unresolved. The latter response would signal concerns in Germany's central bank which the bond market would rather not be reminded of.
(NOTE: The opinions expressed here are those of the writer. They should not be seen as representing the views of Reuters.)
